entities.name: Ibn al‐Ha'im al‐Ishbili
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ibn al‐Ha'im al‐Ishbili, whose full name was Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq al‐Ghafiqi al‐Ishbili, emerged from the vibrant intellectual milieu of Al-Andalus around 1213 as a distinguished Muslim astronomer and mathematician. Operating from Seville during a period of intense scientific exchange and innovation across the Islamic world, his work contributed significantly to the practical application of astronomical tables and mathematical techniques that would influence subsequent generations of scholars in both Islamic and European spheres. His contributions are particularly notable for their precision and their role in refining existing astronomical models, positioning him as a key figure in the transmission of scientific knowledge from the Islamic West.

Ibn al‐Ha'im's primary achievements revolve around his astronomical tables (zij) and his advancements in spherical trigonometry and calendrical calculations. He authored a significant *zij*, likely titled *Kitāb al-Zīj al-Shāmil*, which provided detailed planetary positions, star catalogues, and instructions for calculating prayer times and the direction of Mecca (qibla). This work built upon and refined earlier traditions established by astronomers like al-Zarqali and Jabir ibn Aflah, incorporating observational data and sophisticated mathematical methods to improve accuracy. His treatises often included practical computational methods, demonstrating a strong emphasis on the utility of theoretical astronomy for religious and navigational purposes.
